An ordered grade report partitions units into ordered grades, including strict rankings and reports with ties. Compare how unrestricted, grade-capped, and fixed-order report families grow with unit count.

```{=html}
<div id="app" class="prx-app column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/vendor/d3.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/vendor/plot.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/bundles/how-many-reports.js"></script>
<script>window.__prxApp = PRX["how-many-reports"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("app"));</script>
```

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Three units.** There are 13 ordered grade reports against 6 strict rankings; open **Examples of what is counted** to step through small grade-box partitions.
- **Six units.** All reports reach 4,683, while the cap leaves 603, exact three-grade reports reach 540, and cuts of one declared order leave 32.
- **Eight units.** All reports reach 545,835, compared with 6,051 under the cap and 128 along one order.
- **Twelve units.** Full reports reach 28,091,567,595, while the cap leaves 523,251; hollow squares mark problem sizes used elsewhere on this site.
- **An empty exact family.** At two units and three required grades, 0 reports fit; empty families appear as zero in **Exact counts by n and family**.

<details>
<summary>Declared orders and scope notes</summary>

A report that follows a declared order can cut only between adjacent units in that order. This example has no equal-score blocks. These counts describe the number of eligible reports; posterior risks and search effort depend on the problem and algorithm.

</details>

Standalone: [report counts](../../embed/how-many-reports.html), for example `?n=8&G=3`.
